Azure Striker Gunvolt é um jogo de plataforma 2D claramente inspirado em Mega-Man mas que usa de toques únicos para ser diferente. Normalmente os jogos inspirados de Mega-Man seguem a formula padrão de um jogo da franquia que tão se baseado, usando sistema de chefes como fases e cada chefe derrotado é um poder ou fase nova para você usar e ao derrotar todos os chefes você desbloqueia mais algumas fases em direção ao final com uma das fases tendo algo parecido com um boss rush.

Este jogo não foge muito disso não, ele usa o mesmo sistema de chefes para fases e todo o esquema do final com fases extras guiando até o final mesmo, tendo uma fase com um pseudo boss rush e até o último chefe tendo mais de uma fase tem aqui. Mas o que ele faz diferente é no sistema de armas/poderes por chefes, já que aqui você só um poder de raio e pode ganhar habilidades especiais que se utilizam do raio ou para te auxiliar em outra coisa, como cura a vida, e você só tem uma arma mas com tipos de tiros diferentes e é isso que você vai liberando ao derrotar os chefes, ao menos para mim pareceu que eu liberei por derrotar os chefes.

O jogo possui um sistema de equipamentos também, onde já que você pode trocar o tipo de tiro, você também vai poder adicionar equipamentos que vão te dar efeitos diferentes e pode até conseguir construir equipamentos que fazem isso também, apesar de não ser algo que você deve usar de forma frequente, já que você só ganha itens passando pelas fases e escolhendo opções em algo parecido com Campo Minado mas com escolhas limitadas e não tem bombas, só recompensas, e os itens são todos aleatórios, então pra criar algo especifico você tem que rejogar as fases até conseguir o que você quer.

O jogo tem um sistema de venda de itens e um tipo de dinheiro que só serve pra auxiliar na criação de itens, já que eles custam o dinheiro que você vai ganhando. E também você pode acionar desafios em missões que vão te recompensar itens já descritos nos desafios, então fica como um incentivo pra você repetir missões mais de uma vez e ao menos tempo ajudar a você melhorar no jogo.

A história do jogo é okay. Você é um mercenário de um grupo de rebeldes contra uma grande empresa e faz parte de um grupo seleto de pessoas que tem poderes especiais e um dia, em uma missão que você estava completando você descobre uma garota com as mesmas habilidades que você e que era para você eliminar. Mas ao recusar, você decide sair do seu grupo e virar um mercenário freelancer para cuidar da garota ao mesmo tempo que a empresa está atrás de achar a garota de volta para o seu grande plano.

É uma história meio qualquer coisa e até um pouco fácil de esquecer mas que funciona bem como um pano de fundo para tudo o que ta acontecendo e justifica bem tudo relacionado a gameplay. Como o jogo não é muito grande, dando pra zerar em umas 4 horas ou menos se você não ficar repetindo fases ou morrendo muito, não tinha como se esperar algo tão grandioso, ta na base do que um Mega-Man das antigas seria.

O jogo tem 2 tipos de finais, que você tem que cumprir algumas coisas fáceis de saber o que é quando você vê uma delas, e isso adiciona um fator replay a mais no jogo, já que ao zerar ele uma vez, você no mínimo vai querer ver o final verdadeiro e nisso já vai jogar várias fases de novo para conseguir tudo, e por fim, eu gostei bastante da pixel art do jogo, achei bem feita e bonita. E a arte que aparece durante alguns momentos de história é muito bonita também.

No geral eu gostei do jogo e acho que vale a pena. Só não acho que vale a pena pegar em preço cheio, então espera uma promoção legal e pode ir fundo que em preço promocional vale super a pena. E assim, ele tem uma versão que vem com os 3 jogos da franquia juntos e aparentemente tem coisas a mais nele, então se você ta pensando em qual comprar, a coletânea com os 3 jogos deve valer mais a pena mas se você for como eu que não liga muito pra isso, vai fundo e pode pegar esse mesmo.
The Moral of the story of my past attempt, long ago, to play this game is simple: DON'T EMULATE THE 3DS VERSION OF THE GAME VIA STEAM.

This is really cool and has a lot of interesting ideas! Unfortunately it doesn't nail all of them, but I do respect the effort here. From what I can tell, I've done the final boss, but not the true ending, but I feel like I'm fine leaving it here because the final boss gave me enough trouble to where I'm pretty sure I'll chew my own arms trying to fight something even more challenging.

The visuals here are pretty good! The sprite art especially really stands out as great, both on the main character and the multitude of enemies and bosses you fight. Some of the environments are cool, but I wouldn't say any particularly stand out as really memorable. This sentiment also applies to the music; whilst it isn't *bad* it's nothing particularly standout.

The gameplay here is interesting, and takes a bit of getting used to, but there's certainly a lot of opportunity for skill expression, which I started noticing in the latter half of the game when you're fighting bosses at higher frequency and at much higher difficulty. The boss fights here are pretty cool (even if some of them feel like they have attacks that literally cannot be dodged.) I think the main issues with the gameplay are that the actual stages feel quite basic; they are very corridor heavy with little in the way of platforming; most of the time they just feel like a way to transport you to the boss, rather than a part of a whole experience. The other main problem I noticed was pretty much every effect in this game is some variant of a cool colour; blue, green, grey, white, etc, this means it can be very hard to identify enemy projectiles once you start your electric field attack up (which is the main gimmick of the game.)

I do like the idea of a shop between levels to buy equipment, but having them be trades of loot that you randomly get dropped at the end of a level is quite a mystifying choice; I think it would have been better to just collect one singular currency that you can use to buy and customise your build.

This game definitely has it's strengths, and I am very interested in checking out the sequel as I would like to play more of this with extra polish and refinement. A solid effort here. 6/10

Recomendo – divertido, mas com sistemas mal explicados

Azure Striker Gunvolt é um jogo que, em muitos momentos, lembra bastante a franquia Mega Man, especialmente Mega Man Zero. A jogabilidade é boa, o ritmo funciona e, no geral, é um jogo divertido de ação em 2D que consegue segurar bem o jogador até o final.

Dito isso, o jogo tem problemas claros de design e comunicação com o jogador.

O sistema de builds é praticamente uma roleta russa. Para montar equipamentos eficientes, você depende muito da sorte: conseguir os itens certos, nas quantidades corretas, ou então realizar desafios específicos sem que o jogo deixe claro, de forma objetiva, como tudo isso funciona. Nada é impossível, mas tudo é mal explicado, o que torna o processo mais frustrante do que desafiador.

Outro ponto negativo forte é a falta total de explicação sobre o “Final Verdadeiro”. Se não fosse a internet, simplesmente não haveria como descobrir isso jogando normalmente — especialmente se esse jogo tivesse sido lançado numa época sem fácil acesso a guias e pesquisas online.

Para alcançar o final verdadeiro, o jogador precisa:
– coletar 8 joias
– zerar o jogo uma primeira vez normalmente
– entregar as joias (ou as que faltarem) para a Joule
– usar o colar que ela cria (que não oferece nenhum buff)
– refazer toda a última fase
– derrotar o chefe final usando esse colar

Só então o jogo libera um novo chefe final e o verdadeiro “The End”.

Nada disso é comunicado de forma clara ou intuitiva. O jogo simplesmente espera que o jogador adivinhe ou descubra isso por tentativa, erro ou pesquisa externa.

Particularmente, prefiro jogos com um único final bem construído, ou então múltiplos finais baseados em escolhas claras, como sistemas de karma ou decisões que realmente influenciam a história. Gunvolt não tem isso. Os múltiplos finais aqui não nascem de escolhas narrativas, mas de requisitos obscuros.

Depois que você entende como o jogo funciona — quase fazendo um “curso do SENAI na internet” sobre mecânicas escondidas, sistemas mal explicados ou simplesmente não explicados — Gunvolt finalmente vira um parque de diversão. Mas até chegar nesse ponto, o jogo exige paciência além do razoável.

Resumindo:
– Jogabilidade divertida
– Forte influência de Mega Man (especialmente Zero)
– Combate funciona bem

Mas:
– Sistema de builds confuso
– Dependência excessiva de sorte
– Final verdadeiro mal comunicado
– Design que exige pesquisa externa

Apesar desses problemas, Azure Striker Gunvolt ainda é um bom jogo e merece ser recomendado. Só não espere que ele pegue o jogador pela mão — aqui, aprender dói.

Azure Striker Gunvolt is a refined and stylish 2D action experience that showcases INTI CREATES CO., LTD.’s deep understanding of classic side-scrolling design while confidently pushing the genre forward with modern mechanics and presentation. From the outset, the game establishes a fast, kinetic rhythm built around precision movement, smart offense, and expressive combat systems that reward mastery. Rather than simply emulating its inspirations, it layers new ideas onto a familiar foundation, resulting in a title that feels both nostalgic and distinctly contemporary.

The game’s futuristic setting frames a world where superpowered individuals known as adepts wield extraordinary abilities, and the protagonist, Gunvolt, stands out through his mastery of electricity. This premise provides more than just narrative flavor, as Gunvolt’s powers are deeply integrated into the gameplay loop. Combat revolves around tagging enemies with specialized shots and then letting electrical energy arc toward them automatically, transforming encounters into flowing sequences of movement and positioning rather than static shootouts. This system encourages players to stay mobile, weaving through enemy fire while marking multiple targets before unleashing devastating chained attacks.

Level design supports this combat philosophy by emphasizing momentum and spatial awareness. Stages are constructed to keep players moving forward, blending platforming challenges with enemy placements that test both reflexes and planning. Hazards, vertical sections, and branching paths create a steady sense of escalation, while optional routes reward exploration with resources or higher scoring opportunities. The game rarely slows down, but it avoids feeling overwhelming by clearly communicating enemy patterns and environmental threats, allowing skilled players to enter a satisfying flow state as they advance.

Boss encounters are a defining highlight, each serving as a culmination of the mechanics learned throughout the preceding stage. These fights are visually striking and mechanically demanding, often requiring careful observation and adaptation rather than brute force. Bosses employ distinct attack patterns that push players to fully engage with Gunvolt’s movement options, defensive abilities, and offensive timing. Success feels earned, and repeated attempts naturally lead to improvement as players internalize patterns and refine their approach.

Visually, Azure Striker Gunvolt blends crisp pixel art with dynamic effects that convey speed and power without sacrificing clarity. Characters are animated with fluidity and personality, while environments feature detailed backdrops that reinforce the game’s futuristic tone. Electrical effects, explosions, and boss attacks are vivid and energetic, yet carefully balanced so the screen remains readable even during intense moments. The presentation strikes a strong balance between spectacle and functionality, enhancing immersion without obscuring gameplay.

Sound design plays an equally important role in shaping the experience. The soundtrack is energetic and melodic, reinforcing the game’s sense of urgency and heroism while adapting naturally to different stages and encounters. Sound effects provide clear feedback for player actions, from successful tags to defensive maneuvers, making combat feel responsive and impactful. Voice lines and narrative cues further reinforce character identities, adding emotional texture to what could otherwise be a purely mechanical experience.

Beyond the core action, the game includes progression systems that add depth without overshadowing player skill. Collecting materials and unlocking equipment upgrades allows for subtle customization, letting players fine-tune aspects of Gunvolt’s abilities. These systems complement the main gameplay rather than replacing it, ensuring that success still hinges on execution and understanding rather than statistics alone. For players who enjoy optimization and replayability, these mechanics provide additional incentives to revisit stages and experiment with different approaches.

The narrative unfolds through in-game dialogue and character interactions, leaning heavily into anime-inspired storytelling. While the plot can feel dense or melodramatic at times, it provides context and motivation that enhance the overall journey. The story’s emotional beats, combined with the expressive presentation, help ground the high-speed action in a world that feels inhabited and purposeful, even if not every narrative thread receives equal depth.

Ultimately, Azure Striker Gunvolt stands as a confident and polished action platformer that rewards precision, creativity, and persistence. Its innovative combat systems, strong visual identity, and tightly constructed stages come together to create an experience that remains engaging from beginning to end. For fans of fast-paced 2D action games who appreciate both mechanical depth and stylish presentation, it offers a compelling blend of challenge and spectacle that reflects INTI CREATES’ mastery of the genre.

Rating: 8/10

Azure Striker Gunvolt is a Mega Man–style action platformer built around replayability and score chasing. Its music, art direction, and overall presentation are consistently strong. The story is basic and delivered in a very opaque way, making it easy to miss important details. The game is also short, with a first playthrough taking roughly four to five hours.

At its core, this is a gameplay-first title. Unfortunately, it suffers from critical design issues that undermine its focus on high-score replay. The systems that should encourage mastery clash with poor level design and visibility problems. As a result, it is difficult to recommend outright. However, if you do not care about chasing ranks, are mildly curious about the story, or simply want strong music and creative bosses, the game can still be enjoyable.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]Story[/h2]
The game offers very little exposition and throws you into gameplay almost immediately. This avoids long introductory dialogue but makes the opening confusing. There is minimal setup for the world, characters, or conflict. While the basic plot becomes clearer over time, much of the deeper character history and worldbuilding is only hinted at and rarely explained.

A major issue is how dialogue is delivered during boss fights. The final boss delivers key backstory details while the fight is happening. You can defeat the boss faster than the dialogue finishes, meaning you can easily miss major story revelations. Reading it while dodging attacks is impractical.

This problem is made worse by the language settings. Boss dialogue and in-fight monologues are only visible if you enable English text with Japanese voice acting. If you do not, the dialogue simply does not appear. The game never tells you this, and I was unaware these monologues existed until I saw it mentioned elsewhere.

The game also features two endings. The bad ending is unsatisfying and easy to mistake for a sequel hook. There is little indication that a true ending exists at all. Unlocking it requires collecting specific jewels hidden in stages, which are only marked by a small icon once found. The game never explains what these jewels do or why they matter, making the true ending easy to miss. This is a significant flaw.

While I found the story somewhat interesting, the game discourages engagement with it. You have to hunt for narrative details, replay content in specific ways, and configure settings just to see key dialogue. The result is a player experience that works against story engagement, despite its apparent importance for understanding later entries.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Azure Striker Gunvolt is a run-and-gun platformer built around a unique electricity mechanic. You mark enemies with your gun and then activate an EP surge to electrify them simultaneously. This drains your EP resource and causes you to slowly float downward, adding a layer to combat and platforming. EP is finite and recharges over time. If fully depleted, you are locked out of using it for several seconds.

The game offers a wide range of equippable gear. You can change your gun type and modify your EP ability in meaningful ways. The default setup converts incoming damage into EP loss, but you can equip trade-offs like increased EP damage with faster depletion or reduced damage taken at a cost. Guns vary significantly, encouraging different playstyles. This system is one of the game’s strongest aspects and gives it mechanical depth.

Scoring revolves around a system called Kudos. You build score multipliers by killing multiple enemies simultaneously using the EP surge. Taking damage reduces or resets your Kudos depending on the difficulty mode:

[list]
[*]One hit resets all Kudos.
[*]Three hits reset all Kudos.
[*]Hits do not reset Kudos, but the score multiplier is heavily capped.
[/list]

Achieving high ranks requires constant micromanagement of enemy marking, EP usage, positioning, and avoidance. This demands near-perfect play, but the level design does not support it. Enemies frequently spawn directly on top of you, fall from ceilings without warning, or attack with little telegraphing. The game effectively expects players to memorize placements, spawn timing, and optimal routes through repeated play.

This is further undermined by severe visibility issues. Activating EP darkens the background and fills the screen with bright electrical effects and particles. During these moments, enemy projectiles can become nearly impossible to see. This is especially frustrating because EP usage is central to scoring well. Many hits feel cheap, and you may not know what caused them.

The default EP ability negates damage while EP is available, but this protection does not apply while actively using EP. Almost every time I was hit, it happened during EP activation, when visual clarity was worst.

Boss battles exacerbate these problems. Some attacks lack sufficient telegraphing, and if boss dialogue is enabled, you must read scrolling text while dodging attacks amid heavy visual effects. Losing Kudos due to unavoidable or unclear hits during these moments feels especially punishing given how strict the scoring is.

There are positives. Each stage has a distinct identity and unique mechanics, though many are reused without much variation. Boss designs are visually strong, and fights are generally enjoyable once learned. Some attacks initially seem impossible to dodge but become manageable with practice. Clearer telegraphs would significantly improve fairness.

The quest system is another weak point. You can accept up to three quests per level, but quests reset upon completing the stage. If a quest is not completed, you must manually reaccept it. Objectives are repetitive, usually time limits, rank requirements, or damage restrictions. Completing quests rewards materials used to craft gear and movement options like extra jumps or midair dashes. Many of these feel essential and would have been better as part of the base moveset rather than optional unlocks.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Azure Striker Gunvolt is difficult to recommend due to fundamental issues with level design and visual clarity. The game strongly emphasizes perfect play and high-rank scoring, but achieving this relies more on memorization than skillful reaction. Frequent cheap hits and obstructive visual effects make the scoring system frustrating.

The story, though potentially interesting, is buried behind poor presentation and obscure requirements, making it easier to ignore than engage with. For most players, reading a summary or watching a compilation of cutscenes would provide a better narrative experience.

If you do not care about score chasing and simply want stylish visuals, strong music, and solid boss fights, the game can be enjoyable. Otherwise, its design flaws make it hard to fully recommend.

Azure Striker Gunvolt is Inti Creates returning to what they’re best at: 2D action platformers with tight controls, flashy visuals, and a heavy emphasis on mechanical mastery. At first glance, it might look like another Mega Man-style game, but it plays very differently. While I love the Mega Man Zero series (and even played all the way through to ZX Advent back in the day and once again when the Collection released), I personally ended up enjoying Gunvolt a bit more. That’s just preference, not a claim that one is better than the other—they’re completely different games. Still, since people often compare the two, I think it’s worth pointing out where I stand.

[b]Presentation[/b]
I don’t usually comment on a game’s presentation much since gameplay/story matters more depending on the game, but I’m a sucker for pixel art, so I might be biased—the visuals really add to the appeal. The game’s pixel-art style is sharp and colorful, leaning into anime-inspired character designs and vibrant stage environments. The music is solid for a 2D action-platformer, just what you would expect from an Inti Creates game, but Lumen’s songs are the real highlight for me. It’s a different vibe hearing idol-esque music in this type of game, but it fits perfectly since Lumen is meant to be an idol. I doubt anyone who buys an anime-looking game would be bothered by this type of music—once you hear Beyond the Blue or Reincarnation for the first time, there’s no going back. For anyone who wants to listen to her songs outside the game, you’ll want the Azure Phosphorescence DLC, not the official soundtrack.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
Gunvolt’s gameplay is built around chaining attacks and maintaining high mobility. The core mechanic is tagging enemies with electric markers and unleashing combos, rewarding precision and timing over brute force. Stages are varied, with platforming challenges, environmental hazards, and enemy placement designed to keep you on your toes.

Where the game really pushes back is its scoring system. Beating stages isn’t too hard compared to something like Mega Man Zero, but getting high ranks is brutal. To earn S+ rank, you need mastery of every mechanic: chaining kills, avoiding hits, keeping resources in check, and clearing stages quickly. Some levels are easier than others, but the longer ones will test your consistency and patience. It reminds me of Mega Man Zero’s scoring system, only harsher, since S+ basically demands perfection.

Boss fights are a natural extension of these mechanics. They require adapting your approach rather than memorizing patterns blindly. The encounters feel consistent with the gameplay, and while they vary in length and challenge, they flow naturally from the stages leading up to them.

Gunvolt also rewards replaying stages. Experimenting with different abilities, chaining combos differently, or adjusting movement can improve your rank and open the door to additional challenges. Overall, the game’s structure promotes mastery without feeling overwhelming.

[b]Story[/b]
Gunvolt’s story is surprisingly solid for a 2D action game, blending anime-style dialogue and banter with gameplay. He fights Sumeragi, a corporation controlling Adepts, while protecting Joule, whose powers are being exploited. I know people have gripes with the story in later entries, but this first game’s narrative works on its own. It balances character moments with action and gives Gunvolt a clear motivation, making it one of the most solid stories in the series alongside Luminous Avenger iX.

[b]Major Spoilers Ahead[/b]
Gunvolt begins as a mercenary with QUILL, a group opposing Sumeragi. Early on, he breaks away to rescue Joule from Sumeragi’s control, only to discover her powers remain linked to him. Lumen, a projection of Joule’s Septima, guides and assists him throughout combat and missions.

As the story progresses, Gunvolt confronts several Adept bosses—each unique in style and serving as representatives of Sumeragi’s control over Septima users. They provide challenge and context for the organization’s methods without overwhelming the narrative.

The major twist involves [spoiler]Asimov[/spoiler], Gunvolt’s [spoiler]former mentor[/spoiler] and [spoiler]QUILL’s leader[/spoiler], who is revealed to have his own agenda: [spoiler]using Joule's and Gunvolt's powers for his vision of the world[/spoiler].

The ending depends on stage completion and boss encounters. Failing certain conditions results in a bittersweet conclusion with [spoiler]Joule’s and Gunvolt's deaths[/spoiler]. Completing all requirements unlocks the true ending, where [spoiler]Joule survives in a new form and her connection to Gunvolt is solidified[/spoiler], setting up the foundation for sequels while resolving the first game’s story neatly.

[b]TL;DR: Azure Striker Gunvolt is a fast, challenging 2D action-platformer with tight controls and a brutal scoring system. Its story, while simple, works well, and the colorful pixel-art presentation adds charm. Mastering the mechanics for S+ ranks is tough but rewarding, making it a must-play for fans of precision action.[/b]

[b]Score: 5/10[/b]
[list]
	[*][b]Story:[/b] Very basic and predictable. [spoiler]There's a twist, but anyone paying attention will see it coming a mile away.[/spoiler]
	[*][b]Music:[/b] Decent overall, but nothing stands out. Most tracks are serviceable but not particularly memorable.
	[*][b]Visuals:[/b] The character sprites are extremely pixelated. It's hard to appreciate the art style when the resolution is this low. Text readability also suffers due to the terrible font used throughout the game.
	[*][b]Dialogue:[/b] Most of the dialogue is painfully cringe, filled with melodrama and awkward anime clichés.
	[*][b]Core Combat Mechanic:[/b] The main system—tagging enemies and damaging them with an electric field—is creative and unique. Unfortunately, it would be much more fun if the weapon designs had more depth and the level design made better use of this mechanic.
	[*][b]Combat Flow:[/b] The electric field (your main attack method) is visually overwhelming and often blocks enemy attacks. It feels sloppy and unpolished.
	[*][b]Tutorial:[/b] Core mechanics aren’t explained in-game. You’re expected to either read the manual or press a help button in the main menu. A more organic introduction of mechanics would have been much better.
	[*][b]Level Design:[/b] Aside from a few exceptions, the levels are repetitive and boring. In one level, the same sub-boss is recycled three times—it’s literally the first mini-boss with a different skin.
	[*][b]Enemy Variety:[/b] Very poor enemy variety. You’ll be fighting the same few types over and over again with minimal changes.
	[*][b]Weapons:[/b] There are different main weapons, but most of them are either bad or so situational that they’re not worth using unless you experiment through challenges or look up guides.
	[*][b]Special Abilities:[/b] The special skills are cool and flashy, but you don’t get to choose which one you unlock. It would be much better if you could select them during level-ups.
	[*][b]Bosses:[/b] Most boss fights are a highlight—they're fast-paced, mechanically engaging, and visually interesting. However, the final encounter is poorly designed. It consists of two consecutive phases with no health recovery, no special gauge refill, and no save point in between. This results in unnecessary frustration, especially when retrying after a minor mistake. [spoiler]Worse yet, the true final boss delivers constant dialogue during the fight, making it nearly impossible to follow what’s being said while focusing on intense combat.[/spoiler] 
	[*][b]Crafting System:[/b] Gear crafting is interesting, but getting the materials is not. Materials drop randomly at the end of stages, and the quantity depends on picking up hidden items during the level—but there's always a fixed base amount. You can also get items from challenges, but since this forces you to replay the same stages multiple times, the whole process becomes tedious quickly.
	[*][b]Challenges:[/b] Challenges seem to get deselected if you don’t complete them in the next mission. Poor design that makes the whole system frustrating to engage with.
	[*][b]Difficulty Modes:[/b] The game includes multiple modes—easy, hard, and one specifically aimed at speedrunners. Adds some replay value depending on your preferred playstyle.
	[*][b]Saving System:[/b] There is no autosave. The game warns you about this, but that doesn’t make it any less annoying. One crash or mistake and you lose a lot of progress.
	[*][b]Configuration Options:[/b] Very limited. It lacks basic customization features you’d expect in a PC port.
	[*][b]Recommendation:[/b] Might be worth checking out if you're a fan of old-school Mega Man-style games or if you're into speedrunning. Otherwise, it’s a rough ride.
[/list]

This is a difficult game to review, as I was looking forward to getting to it in my backlog only to be immensely disappointed.  At first some odd bugs with the keybinds that I was experiencing kept the dash button from working at all.

Gameplay is close enough to Megaman X/Zero that the mechanical differences make it very difficult to play, like not being able to wall-cling.  Years of muscle memory will backfire on you.
- The Tag and Zap gameplay is very unnatural and unsatisfying as a consequence.  It feels like something that should have been removed or changed during prototyping.
- Flashfield's visual effects and ability to block some but not all attacks can mask subtle damaging attacks until you learn to look through it and even then it's still visually distracting.
- The "prevasion" mechanic dissociates causes of damage in your mind and makes it easy to learn bad habits in places because you think you've dodged something or blocked it with flashfield only for it to have really hit you.  I really hope they removed this entirely in GV2 and beyond.
- Bosses all seem to have patterns that cannot be dodged, such as the Danmaku pattern on fire boss.  I had greatly enjoyed the Megaman Zero games for being well designed and fair, but this game seems to revel in the base unit of difficulty being "cruel and unusual mechanics meant to challenge Megaman Zero speedrunners".
- There's an entire "Farm materials to craft gear" system that you can basically just... skip.  One entire gear slot is going to be worthless in the last stage, and for all the options in the ring slot you can't craft the best ones until you beat the last stage.  I spent some time trying to farm gear and the RNG at the end of each stage just made it a poor investment of time.  Farming nightmare souls in Megaman X6 was more respectful of your time and effort.

The Story is nothing to write home about.  Gunvolt is the overlap on the Venn Diagram of X-men and Guilty Crown.  The bad translation further confounds this with a bunch of absolutely random and senseless name changes that make the JP voice/EN text option jarring.  (at least I knew in advance to go into language and switch it to the "new" translation which is less bad but still takes perverse delight in changing virtually every name in the story.  What madness compelled them to do this?)  [strike][b]Acura was right.[/b][/strike]

The Music is nice, I quite enjoyed the "Anthem" tracks where Morpho starts singing.  I would put the music at a solid 7/10.  A lot of it blends into the game smoothly, nothing really stands out until the lyrics kick in.

Overall I would watch the game's story on Youtube and save yourself some wrist pain and a ton of frustration.  I need to play the second game to see if I would recommend skipping to it or just passing on the series, but this first game is 8 hours of stupid.

[h1]スコアアタックが熱いビリビリアクション  [/h1]
神作『ロックマン９』を作り上げた開発、インティクリエイツのＩＰ。さすがというか評判どおりの出来だった、これは面白い。

まず言いたいのは、00年代のライトノベル文化を下地としたオタクアニメ成熟期のあの時代感覚、そこに着目したコンセプトアートはお見事（"ビリビリ中学生"やらデジロック的挿入歌やら『電磁砲』を彷彿とさせるが、個人的に終始『灼眼のシャナ』を想起していた）。
変哲もない横スクロールアクションと思いきや、従来のシューティングスタイルから一歩踏み出し、ロックオン→ビリビリ→撃破のルーチンが新鮮で楽しい。
敵にビリビリしつつもう一方の敵にロックオンしたりそのまま前進したり、基本的にアクションが途絶えることがない中々秀逸な発明だと感じた。
ボスキャラも皆一癖あって、ポップなキャラ付けからくる軽い印象から一転悲惨な背景が垣間見えたりと、軸となるストーリーも相俟っていちいち心に残る。
サウンド面では、一定のスコアを超えると挿入歌が流れ、演出もさることながら曲としても良質だった。
アニソンに歌謡曲のスパイスを足したようなトラックはとても印象的。
「霧時計」、「追憶の心傷」、「碧き扉」がお気に入り。

『ガンヴォルト』は今や三作目まで発売されていることからもわかるように、既にこの頃から一大コンテンツとなるパワーは存分に発揮されている（しかもその最新作が最高傑作と呼ぶ声もあるのだから恐ろしい）。

ところでこのゲーム、わりかしアクションゲームにそこそこ自信を持っていた私のプライドをズタボロにしたゲームでもある。
断っておくがクリア自体（真END含む）はおそらく誰でもできる。それこそアクションが鬼門でも救済措置は多くあるので。
問題はやり込み、いわゆる実績コンプである（トロコンとも）。
ミッションの最高ランクを取得するにはほぼノーダメ＆スピードランが要求されるのだが、ノーダメノーミスが大のニガテである私はここでかなり打ちのめされた。
とはいえ前述したようにこのゲームには救済措置があり、なんなら得点をサポートするアイテムやメソッドなんかも用意されており、私はなんとかそれを頼りに制覇できた（思えば救済措置をどのように利用すれば高得点を狙えるか思考していたときが、最も楽しかったかもしれない）。

繰り返すけれどスコアタはストーリー進行に必須ではないのでご安心を。
実績コンプ目指すプレイヤーは沼らないよう注意。SPミッションは中継地点が無いのでミスると中々に心折られる。
全体的な満足感は相当なもの。超オススメ。
